note: Enterprise GPU-server acquisition prices, per SPEC 5.8. THERE IS NO first_party TIER IN THIS FILE, and unlike gpu-pricing.json there never can be one from a free endpoint: Dell, HPE and Supermicro publish no machine-readable list price for a GPU server, and Supermicro's own store is configure-to-order with no public per-config figure. Rows are therefore one of TWO tiers, both defined in `tiers` and neither a quote: `indicative` — a published integrator or analyst figure, carried with the exact sentence it was taken from; or `derived_component` — a band CONSTRUCTED from a cited card price and a cited GPU cost-share, for accelerators where no integrator publishes a system price at all. scripts/build-server-pricing.mjs re-fetches every cited page and proves each citation still holds, and additionally recomputes each derived band from its own stated inputs.

tiers.indicative: A published integrator/analyst figure. Planning band, not a quote. No vendor list price exists to promote it to.
tiers.derived_component: NOT a published system price — no integrator publishes one for this configuration. Constructed from two cited figures: a published price for the ACCELERATOR, and a published statement of what share of a build's cost the GPUs represent. It is a planning band with an auditable derivation, and it is strictly WEAKER than `indicative`: the share figure was stated about builds in general, not about this exact configuration. Every such row carries `derivation` (inputs + formula, so the band can be recomputed and falsified) and `derived_from` (one citation per input). The UI MUST NOT present these rows as published integrator figures.

disagreement_note: Two independent sources are carried for the SAME configuration where both publish one, and they disagree by up to 22% on an 8xH100 node ($250-320K vs $310-370K). Both ship as separate rows. They are NOT averaged: the mean of two published bands is a figure neither source states, and it would read as more authoritative than either while being citable to nothing. The calculator shows the spread and lets the buyer pick a row.
derived_component_note: This tier exists because the alternative was worse. RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell has no published integrated-node price at ANY multi-GPU tier: the one integrator publishing a tier table (VRLA Tech) prices only its entry and single-card tiers and marks dual, quad and 8-GPU as `Configured to workload`. Its single published RTX PRO 6000 figure, `Starting at $5,999`, is BELOW the $16,000 the same card lists for on NVIDIA's own marketplace — on a page that itself states the GPU is 50-70% of the build. Seeding that would have put a system in this registry priced under its own GPU. So the choice was an auditable construction or no rows at all, and a construction that says exactly what it is beats a published figure that is provably wrong.
coverage_note: h100, h200 and b200 carry `indicative` rows read off published integrator figures. rtx_pro_6000_ws and rtx_pro_6000_se carry `derived_component` rows instead, because no integrator publishes a system price for this card at any multi-GPU tier. The remaining accelerators in gpu-pricing.json (a100_80, a100_40, l40s, l4, a10, a10g, h20, a800) have no server row at all, so they derive NO capex and the UI says so. An accelerator with no server row is a stated coverage gap, never a silently borrowed price from a neighbouring card — and a `derived_component` row is a stated CONSTRUCTION, never a discovered quote.
verification_note: Each row's `verification` records whether its quoted sentence was still present at source_url when this file was generated. verified = the citation holds. citation_broken = the page changed; the figure is retained with its original observed_at and MUST be rendered as unverified. unreachable = the fetch failed, which is a network fact about this run, not a judgement on the figure. A `derived_component` row is checked against EVERY citation it carries and takes the WEAKEST result, with the per-input outcomes in `verification.citations` — so a row whose card price still verifies but whose cost-share sentence has moved reports broken, not verified. Those rows are ALSO re-derived at build time: the seeded band must reproduce from the row's own `derivation` inputs or the build fails outright, which is a stronger check than any citation test and the reason the tier is admissible at all.

excludes: the dedicated 20A 208-240V circuit this card's 600W envelope needs

derivation.formula: cards_usd = card_usd * gpu_count; usd_low = round(cards_usd * 100 / gpu_share_high_pct); usd_typical = round(cards_usd * 100 / gpu_share_typical_pct); usd_high = round(cards_usd * 100 / gpu_share_low_pct). The HIGH share yields the LOW system price: if the GPUs are 70% of the build, the rest of the build is small.
derivation.typical_basis: The 60% share is the midpoint of the cited 50-70% range. Same treatment the Chinese-cloud rows in gpu-pricing-seed.json already give a cited band, and it is stated here rather than presented as a published figure.

derived_from.note: Reports NVIDIA's own marketplace listing for the Workstation Edition, September 2026. The card launched at an $8,565 MSRP in March 2025; the rise is attributed to the GDDR7 shortage, so this input is volatile and is the first thing to re-check.
Stated by the integrator about its AI workstation builds in general, NOT about this configuration specifically. This is the weaker of the two inputs and the reason the tier is not `indicative`.

rows.note: The single-card workstation is the entry buy for this accelerator: 96GB on one card runs a 70B model at FP8 without tensor-parallel at all, which is the whole reason it is interesting against an H100. The band is wide by construction because the cost share it divides by is wide.

derivation.formula: cards_usd = card_usd * gpu_count; usd_low = round(cards_usd * 100 / gpu_share_high_pct); usd_typical = round(cards_usd * 100 / gpu_share_typical_pct); usd_high = round(cards_usd * 100 / gpu_share_low_pct). derived_from.note: A JUNE 2026 average for the Server Edition, deliberately three months older than the September figure used on the Workstation rows, because no September Server Edition price met the citation bar. GDDR7 prices rose across that window, so this band probably UNDERSTATES a September buy. Carried as-is rather than adjusted upward — an adjustment would be a figure no source states, the same rule that keeps the two disagreeing 8xH100 sources unaveraged.

WEAKEST link in this row. The share is stated about workstation-class builds; a rackmount server with redundant PSUs and IPMI plausibly carries proportionally more non-GPU cost, which would push the true price toward or past the high bound. An 8-GPU row was deliberately NOT seeded for exactly this reason.

rows.note: The smaller serving stack: 384GB across four cards, which is the point where this accelerator competes with a 4x H100 PCIe node at roughly half the capex. Server Edition is the passive-cooled part and the one every cloud provider rents, so its rented and owned rows describe the same silicon.
